description: Rock evidence for Earth's major swings between frozen icehouse and warm greenhouse states.
content_html:
A Planet That Has Changed Its Mind

Earth’s climate has never been fixed. Over hundreds of millions of years, the planet has swung between two extremes: icehouse conditions — when ice sheets spread across the continents — and greenhouse conditions — when the planet was so warm that ice barely existed even at the poles. These dramatic shifts are recorded in the rock record, and geologists read them like the pages of a climate history book.

Understanding past climate states is one of the most powerful tools in geology. If you know the conditions under which a rock formed, you can reconstruct where on Earth that area sat, what the sea level was doing, and how the atmosphere was behaving at the time. This lesson focuses on the two key states and the rocks that provide the evidence for each.

Key Fact

Tillite is the key rock evidence for icehouse conditions. It is lithified (solidified) glacial till — a jumbled, poorly sorted mixture of sand, pebbles and boulders dropped directly by ice. Finding tillite in a region tells geologists that glaciers once covered that area, even if the region sits in the tropics today.

Icehouse Earth: Evidence from Tillites

The Carboniferous and Permian periods (roughly 360–250 million years ago) represent a major icehouse phase. At that time, the supercontinent Gondwana sat over the South Pole, and enormous glaciers spread across what is now South America, Africa, Antarctica, India and Australia. As these continents drifted northward over geological time, the tillites they carried moved with them. Today, Carboniferous tillites are found in South America and southern Africa — regions that are now tropical or temperate, far from any ice.

Tillites are identified by several features that distinguish them from other poorly sorted rocks. The fragments are angular rather than rounded, showing they were not transported by water (which rounds particles). They show no layering or grading because glaciers dump all particle sizes together without any sorting. Striated (scratched) pebbles and polished bedrock surfaces beneath tillites are further evidence that ice dragged rocks across the landscape. In your exam, identifying tillite as evidence of glaciation — and explaining why its poor sorting and angular clasts indicate a glacial origin — is a high-value skill.

Students sometimes confuse tillite with other poorly sorted sedimentary rocks such as conglomerate or breccia. The key differences are: (1) conglomerates contain rounded clasts (water-transported), whereas tillite clasts are angular; (2) breccias have angular clasts but typically show better sorting and are deposited by gravity flows (screes, landslides), not by ice; (3) tillite contains a chaotic mixture of clay, sand and boulders with no grading or layering — a signature of direct glacial deposition. Striated surfaces on individual clasts are unique to glacial environments and are the clinching piece of evidence.

Greenhouse Earth: Evidence from Limestones and Chalk

Greenhouse conditions are recorded by a very different set of rocks. When global temperatures were high and ice was absent, sea levels rose because no water was locked in polar ice sheets. Warm, shallow seas spread across low-lying continental areas. In these conditions, limestone accumulated as marine organisms such as corals, brachiopods and crinoids built their shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate dissolved in the warm water.

The British area provides a compelling record of these greenhouse phases. During the Carboniferous period (before the full glaciation of Gondwana reached its maximum), warm tropical seas covered much of Britain, depositing the Carboniferous Limestone that forms the Yorkshire Dales, the Mendips and the Peak District today. Fossil corals found in these rocks — species that only live in warm, shallow tropical water — confirm that Britain sat near the equator at the time, in greenhouse-like conditions.

Key Fact

Chalk is a pure white limestone made almost entirely of the microscopic remains of coccolithophores — tiny floating algae. Chalk formed during the Cretaceous period (roughly 145–66 million years ago), a profound greenhouse phase when global temperatures were 6–10°C warmer than today and sea levels were 100–200 m higher than at present. The White Cliffs of Dover, the North and South Downs, and the Yorkshire Wolds are all made of Cretaceous Chalk.

Latitude Change and the British Record

One of the most important insights from comparing icehouse and greenhouse rocks in Britain is that the rock type alone is not enough — latitude change through plate movement must be considered too. Britain has drifted northward over geological time. During the Lower Palaeozoic (Cambrian to Devonian, roughly 540–360 million years ago), what is now Britain sat in the southern hemisphere tropics or subtropics, so warm-water carbonates and reef limestones are found in Wales and Scotland from this era.

By the Cenozoic (66 million years ago to the present), Britain had reached its current mid-latitude position. The most recent icehouse phase — the Pleistocene glaciations, beginning about 2.6 million years ago — left behind boulder clays, drumlins and glacial erratics across Scotland, northern England and Wales. These form the youngest glacial record in the British sequence and sit directly above older greenhouse-phase sediments, dramatically illustrating how climate and plate position have both changed over deep time.

Students often assume that if a tropical rock (such as reef limestone) is found in Scotland, it simply means Scotland was once warm. This conflates two separate factors. Latitude change through plate tectonics is one driver — Scotland was once near the equator. But global climate state matters too: during a full greenhouse phase, even mid-latitude areas have warm climates, whereas during an icehouse phase, even equatorial regions can be cooler than today’s tropics. A complete exam answer distinguishes between these two effects and addresses both when interpreting British rock sequences.

Reading the Rock Record as a Climate Archive

The value of the icehouse–greenhouse framework is that it connects rock type, fossil content, latitude history, and global sea level into a single coherent narrative. Tillites tell you ice was present; limestones and chalk tell you warm, shallow seas prevailed. Together, they reveal that Earth has experienced multiple icehouse and greenhouse phases through its 4.54-billion-year history — and that the planet’s climate is capable of extreme swings on timescales of tens of millions of years.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to identify evidence for an icehouse or greenhouse period, name the rock type and then explain what feature of it proves the climate interpretation — for tillite, it is the poor sorting, angular clasts and striated surfaces; for limestone or chalk, it is the warm-water marine fossils and the conditions required for calcium carbonate to accumulate. Simply naming the rock without explaining the evidence will not earn full marks. If the question asks you to compare icehouse and greenhouse conditions, you must address both in each point you make — for example “icehouse rocks are tillites with angular unsorted clasts, whereas greenhouse rocks are limestones formed from warm-water marine organisms.”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Icehouse conditions are evidenced by tillites — poorly sorted, angular, unsorted glacial deposits that record the presence of continental ice sheets, such as Carboniferous tillites in South America and Africa.
  • Greenhouse conditions are evidenced by limestones (including chalk) — warm-water carbonate rocks formed in shallow seas when global temperatures were high and ice was absent, such as Cretaceous Chalk across southern England.
  • Both latitude change through plate tectonics and global climate state must be considered when interpreting past rock sequences in Britain — the two factors act together and must not be confused.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following rock types provides the best evidence for a past icehouse period?
A) Oolitic limestone
B) Chalk
C) Tillite
D) Coal
Identify one feature of tillite that distinguishes it from a water-deposited conglomerate.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any of: angular (not rounded) clasts / poorly sorted with no grading / chaotic mix of clay, sand and boulders / presence of striated clasts [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how chalk forms and what climate conditions its presence indicates.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for describing formation (accumulated from microscopic coccolithophore remains / calcium carbonate microfossils settling on the seafloor in warm shallow seas). One mark for climate indication (greenhouse conditions / high global temperatures / sea level significantly higher than today / absence of polar ice) [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why Carboniferous tillites are found in South America and Africa today, even though those regions are now tropical.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that during the Carboniferous, South America and Africa were part of Gondwana, which sat over the South Pole; plate tectonics has since moved these landmasses to lower latitudes, carrying the tillites with them; therefore the present-day latitude of the rock does not reflect the latitude at which it was deposited.
Secure: Identifies Gondwana over the South Pole and plate movement northward, but explanation of the mismatch between present and past latitude is less fully developed.
Developing: States that the landmasses used to be at higher latitudes / further south, without clearly linking to Gondwana or plate tectonics.
Emerging: States that it was cold in the past without explaining plate movement. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A geologist finds a sequence of rocks in Wales that includes Carboniferous Limestone overlain by Carboniferous tillite. Explain what this sequence tells us about the change in climate during the Carboniferous period.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that the limestone below indicates earlier warm, shallow marine greenhouse conditions; the tillite above indicates a shift to icehouse conditions with glaciation; cross-cutting relationships show the change was from warmer to colder, linking to the southward position of Gondwana and the growth of polar ice sheets.
Secure: Identifies both rock types and links each to greenhouse/icehouse conditions; explains the sequence as a climate cooling event.
Developing: Identifies one rock type correctly with the correct climate; does not fully develop the change or the sequence.
Emerging: States that the sequence shows climate change without linking rock types to conditions. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how effectively the rock record can be used to reconstruct past climate states on Earth. In your answer, refer to specific rock types and the evidence they provide.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates the rock record as a powerful but incomplete climate archive. Strengths: tillites provide unambiguous evidence of past glaciation (poor sorting, angular clasts, striated surfaces); limestones and chalk record warm shallow marine conditions (warm-water fossils, high sea level); the sequence of rock types through time allows climate changes to be detected. Limitations: plate tectonic movement means rock latitude must be corrected before climate interpretation; some rock types (e.g. coal) form under a range of conditions and are less diagnostic; erosion removes parts of the record. Reaches a reasoned conclusion.
Secure: Covers at least two rock types with specific evidence, addresses one strength and one limitation, reaches a conclusion.
Developing: Describes rock types and their climate association but does not evaluate or discuss limitations.
Emerging: Makes simple points about climate change in rock record without specific rock evidence. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which rock type is direct evidence of past glaciation?
What is the main constituent of chalk?
Tillite is poorly sorted and has _____ clasts because it was deposited directly by ice rather than by water.
During the Cretaceous period, global sea levels were _____ than today because ice was absent.
Match each rock type to the climate state it records:

flashcard_questions.q: What is tillite and how does it form?
flashcard_questions.a: Lithified glacial till — a poorly sorted mix of clay, sand and boulders deposited directly by ice.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are tillite clasts angular rather than rounded?
flashcard_questions.a: They were not transported by water, which rounds particles; ice carries and drops them without abrasion.

flashcard_questions.q: What climate state does tillite indicate?
flashcard_questions.a: Icehouse conditions — the presence of continental ice sheets.

flashcard_questions.q: The chalk of the White Cliffs of Dover formed during which geological period?
flashcard_questions.a: The Cretaceous period (roughly 145–66 million years ago).

flashcard_questions.q: Cretaceous chalk is made almost entirely from the remains of which organisms?
flashcard_questions.a: Coccolithophores — microscopic planktonic algae with calcium carbonate plates.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the presence of chalk tell geologists about sea levels at the time of its formation?
flashcard_questions.a: Sea levels were 100–200 m higher than today because no water was locked in polar ice.

flashcard_questions.q: Carboniferous tillites are found in South America today. Why does this not mean South America was once polar?
flashcard_questions.a: South America was part of Gondwana, which sat over the South Pole; plate movement has since carried it to tropical latitudes.

flashcard_questions.q: What two factors must a geologist consider when interpreting past climate from British rocks?
flashcard_questions.a: Both global climate state (icehouse or greenhouse) and latitude change through plate tectonics.

flashcard_questions.q: Carboniferous Limestone in the Yorkshire Dales contains fossil corals. What does this imply about Britain's past latitude?
flashcard_questions.a: Britain sat near the equator during the Carboniferous, in warm tropical seas.

flashcard_questions.q: How does limestone differ from tillite as a climate indicator?
flashcard_questions.a: Limestone records warm shallow marine greenhouse conditions; tillite records cold glacial icehouse conditions.

flashcard_questions.q: What feature on individual pebbles within tillite confirms glacial origin?
flashcard_questions.a: Striations — scratches made when ice dragged rocks across bedrock.
A streamlined hill of glacial till deposited beneath an ice sheet.

glossary_terms.definition: A prolonged period of Earth history when global temperatures were low, ice sheets covered large parts of the continents, and sea levels were reduced.
A prolonged period of Earth history when global temperatures were high, polar ice was absent or minimal, and warm shallow seas covered much of the land.
A sedimentary rock made of poorly sorted angular fragments of all sizes, deposited directly by glaciers without the sorting action of water or wind.
A sedimentary rock composed chiefly of calcium carbonate (CaCO3), often formed from the remains of marine organisms such as corals, shells and microfossils in warm shallow seas.
Microscopic planktonic algae with calcium carbonate plates (coccoliths) that floated in warm Cretaceous seas and settled to form chalk after death.

items.description: Clear explainer on the most extreme icehouse state in Earth's history — useful for understanding the scale of glaciation recorded by tillites.

items.title: Frozen Planet (BBC, 2011)
items.description: Attenborough's landmark series on polar ice environments — stunning footage of the ice sheets and glacial landscapes that tillites preserve a record of.

items.title: Chasing Ice (2012)
items.description: Photographer James Balog documents retreating glaciers over years — brings icehouse-to-greenhouse transition to life in real time.

items.title: Planet Earth (BBC, 2006)
items.description: Episodes covering polar and mountain environments show the geological landscapes shaped by the Pleistocene glaciation, the most recent icehouse phase.

items.title: British Geological Survey — Discovering Geology
items.description: BGS education hub covering UK rock sequences including Carboniferous limestone and chalk — the two key greenhouse-period rock types in this lesson.

items.description: Free classroom activities including exercises on interpreting rock sequences as climate evidence — directly relevant to icehouse and greenhouse analysis.

items.title: NASA Earth Observatory — Ice Ages
items.description: NASA's accessible explanation of what drives ice ages and how geologists read past climate states from the rock and ice record.

items.title: The Geological Society — Climate Change: Evidence
items.description: The Geological Society's overview of rock-based evidence for past climate change, covering tillites, chalk and other key indicators.
